# Decision Index

Decisions live inside long documents under eight identifier namespaces with no
index (`D*`, `A*`, `R-*`, `S*`, `C.*`, `E.*`, `M*`, `DEC-*`), and production
modules used to cite section numbers of a spec since superseded. Rules are
versionless; section numbers are not. This file is the index for the four
namespaces that carry live, enforced decisions: `D*` (topology), `A*` (audit
amendments), `R-*` (guardrail rules), `DEC-*` (architecture). `S*`, `C.*`,
`E.*`, `M*` are structural/procedural section labels inside
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-nora-strands-spec.md`, not decisions in
their own right, and are not indexed here.

See `ARCHITECTURE.md` for the map this index supports, and each identifier's
defining document for the full rationale — this file is deliberately terse.

**Deprecated rows.** A row whose subject has been deleted is **marked
`DEPRECATED`, never renumbered and never removed** — every cross-reference in
`design/dreamer-agent-loop/` and in the specs points at a number, so reusing or
reflowing one silently rewrites history. As of **2026-09-07** the knowledge tier
(the "fact tier") and the language tier are deprecated and their code deleted
(issue #115); the rows marked below are theirs. Their database tables are **not**
dropped by that change — the code goes, the schema stays, and dropping them is a
separate explicit decision. The evidence is in
`design/dreamer-agent-loop/20-knowledge-tier.md` §0.

## D — Topology (`design/00-overview.md`)

| ID | Statement | Enforcing test |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Ambient ingest never passes through the Agent SDK; the SDK is constructed, invoked, and discarded once per tag. **Amended by A3** (see below): the ambient path may later host a lightweight relevance classifier, still not the full Agent SDK. **Revised 2026-09-05 (design/dreamer-agent-loop/35):** an untagged message in an operator-opted-in room may reach the full model ONCE per quiescence-closed window, through the participation occasion on `FirePath.speak` — the first exception, occasion-gated, with the right to silence. Ordinary ambient traffic is unchanged. | `test_ambient_reaches_the_agent_only_through_participation_gating` (R-1) |
| D2 | SQLite is an audit record, not the semantic store; Honcho is the semantic store (peer cards, relationships, durable recall). | no dedicated test — a schema-level property |
| D3 | The Strands Agents SDK is the tagging-path engine — no hand-rolled loop, context builder, or session store. | `test_strands_import_boundary` (structural: only `nora/agent/**` may import `strands`) |
| D4 | Every tag is a fresh, stateless agent invocation; continuity comes from SQLite + Honcho pre-filled into context, never SDK session persistence. **Amended by DEC-3**: the injection invariant holds, but an additive, TTL'd `Episode` concept is accepted for later — not implemented in stage 1. | no dedicated test (statelessness itself); `tests/integration/test_statelessness.py` exercises the invariant |
| D5 | Everything identity-related (trigger text, account, peer mapping, model, endpoints) is config, never hardcoded. | `tests/test_config.py` (`extra="forbid"`, no hardcoded identity fields) |
| D6 | Peer mapping is manual, one operator-maintained file — no service, no UI. **Amended by A2**: two-level mapping (`person_id` → name + per-platform sender IDs), one person = one Honcho peer across platforms. **`design/04`'s identity-discovery mechanism is further amended by DEC-9**: identity discovery moves onto the `PlatformAdapter` port (`resolve_identity()`), not read from a private adapter attribute. | `test_self_tag_ignored` (R-12, depends on identity resolution); `tests/test_persons.py` | **Further amended by DEC-14/DEC-16 (Phase 8)**: the file now maps one person to many ACCOUNTS per platform, not one id per platform; and while it stays hand-edited — Nora never writes it — adoption is now *lazy*, so an edit plus a restart backfills that person's pre-mapping messages into Honcho rather than leaving a permanent hole. `nora persons pending` only ever suggests; it writes nothing.

## R-1…R-17 — Enforced guardrail rules

Source of truth for the rule statements and the assigned test names:
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-03-nora-strands-spec.md` §B.1. The registry of
which named test satisfies which rule is `tests/test_acceptance_rules.py::RULE_TESTS`
— that dict, not this table, is what `test_every_enforced_rule_has_a_named_test`
checks against; this table is sourced from it, not the reverse.

| ID | Statement | Enforcing test |
|---|---|---|
| R-1 | **Only the tagging path and the heartbeat's fire path may cause a send; ambient traffic reaches the agent only through the participation occasion's gating.** *Revised 2026-08-08 (DEC-69). The old wording, preserved: “Only the tagging path may cause a send; ambient traffic never reaches the agent.” Revised again 2026-09-05 (design/dreamer-agent-loop/35): the SECOND clause's first-ever revision — an untagged message in an operator-opted-in room may now reach the agent, once per quiescence-closed window, through `FirePath.speak`, with the right to silence. Ordinary ambient traffic still constructs zero agents, and the renamed test still pins that.* The first clause changed because `nora.app.fire.FirePath` is a send **not caused by a tag** — Nora's first unprompted-speech path. What did NOT change is that the set of senders is closed and enumerated: it went from one to two, by decision, and a third is a rule change rather than a new module. The participation occasion is not a third sender: it speaks THROUGH the fire path, so R-1b's two callers remain two. **Amended 2026-09-28 by DEC-219** (`design/cognition-loop` step 0): cognition sends nothing directly; its acts are reminder rows the fire path sends. | `test_ambient_reaches_the_agent_only_through_participation_gating` |
| R-1b | **AMENDED 2026-09-25 by DEC-212: `deliver.build` has a third caller, the public Instagram summons (`nora/app/summons.py`), which holds its text and never reaches an adapter.** **The tag path and the fire path are the only two senders, structurally.** R-1's revised first clause needed its own test and could not reuse R-1's: `test_ambient_reaches_the_agent_only_through_participation_gating` asserts the ambient clause but harnesses only AMBIENT input, so a reminders fire path never enters it and it stayed green while the rule changed underneath it — amending the row alone would have deleted the only written brake on a third send path with nothing going red. Three AST facts, one per link in the chain: `Deliverer` is the only caller of `adapter.send` (so R-2's latch, R-4, R-6's leak scan, R-18's egress scan and A9's audit-first write cannot be bypassed), `Deliverer` is constructed only by `deliver.build` (where `audience` has no default), and `deliver.build` has exactly two callers. The participation occasion (design/dreamer-agent-loop/35) goes through `FirePath.speak`, so this row is untouched by it. **Amended 2026-09-28 by DEC-220** (`design/cognition-loop` step 0): unchanged — cognition adds no sender. **Amended 2026-10-05 by DEC-287:** a fourth caller, the one-time code (`nora/app/otp.py`): a fixed template, no model, into a direct message to somebody in `identity.toml` (R-101), through `deliver.build` so every guard and the audit-first write still apply. | `test_only_the_tag_path_and_the_fire_path_can_send` |
| R-2 | **One tag produces one turn, and a turn produces at most `NATIVE_TOOLS["send_reply"].budget` messages, all to the tagging conversation.** *Revised 2026-08-07 (DEC-40). The old wording, preserved: “`send_reply` executes at most once per tag, counting attempts, not successes.”* The invariant was never the number one — it is that a tag cannot produce unbounded output and cannot produce output anywhere but where it was tagged. The second half is untouched (`send_reply` still goes to the deliverer's bound target — DEC-21, R-3), and “counting attempts, not successes” is untouched: a failed send still spends a message, because there is no auto-retry. What changed is that the bound is a NUMBER read from the tool table rather than the literal 1, and **that budget is still 1 as shipped**, so behaviour is byte-identical until an operator raises it. | `test_second_send_reply_is_cancelled` |
| R-2b | The `Deliverer` latch is bounded by `message_cap`, independent of `ReplyGuard` — and `message_cap` is the SAME number, read out of the same `ToolRegistry.budgets()` mapping by `nora.engagement.stages.deliver.build`. *Revised 2026-08-07 (DEC-40); previously “single-shot”, which at a cap of 1 is the same sentence.* | `test_deliverer_latch_is_single_shot` |
| R-3 | `send_reply` may only target the conversation that produced the tag. **Mechanism changed 2026-08-05 (DEC-21): held BY CONSTRUCTION, not by veto.** Both scoped tools ignore the model's `conversation_id` — `read_buffer` reads the closure value (Task 1's cross-group leak fix) and `send_reply` calls `deliverer.deliver(text)`, whose `Deliverer` binds its target at construction — so the argument is inert and nothing the model writes can change where a message goes. That is strictly stronger than the old check, which could be satisfied by a model echoing the right string. A mismatch is counted as `nora_tool_scope_violations_total{tool}`, not vetoed. **Mechanism narrowed again 2026-08-06 (DEC-24): the argument no longer exists.** No tool declares a conversation parameter, so the model is never asked for one; the counter now fires only when a model supplies an OUT-OF-SCHEMA `conversation_id` (which Strands drops during validation), on any tool, and never on a well-formed call. | `test_send_to_other_group_cannot_escape_the_tagged_conversation` |
| R-4 | Empty or whitespace-only reply text is never delivered. | `test_empty_reply_not_sent` |
| R-5 | No error text ever reaches the group — silent failure, always. | `test_silent_failure_matrix` |
| R-6 | No reply may contain the canary token, a verbatim ≥40-character span of the assembled doctrine text, or the prompt's transcript markup (`<m n=…>`, which a member's escaped body cannot produce). | `test_leak_guard_blocks_canary`, `test_a_reply_quoting_the_transcript_markup_is_refused` |
| R-6b | ...and a verbatim doctrine span specifically. | `test_leak_guard_blocks_doctrine_verbatim` |
| R-6c | A normal, non-leaking reply is never blocked by the leak guard. | `test_leak_guard_allows_normal_reply` |
| R-7 | Per-tag tool-call budget (`read_buffer` ≤ 2, `read_peer_card` ≤ 1, `send_reply` ≤ 1); unknown tools default-deny. **DEC-10** [built, agent/tool-registry phase]: the budget table is now injected — `ReplyGuard(budgets=...)` reads `nora.agent.registry.ToolRegistry.budgets()`, threaded through `nora.engagement.stages.deliver.build` — instead of a hardcoded `ReplyGuard.BUDGETS` class attribute. Unknown-tool default-deny (the other half of this rule) is unchanged: a tool absent from `budgets` is still vetoed. | `test_tool_call_budget_enforced_for_read_buffer` (budget half); `test_an_unknown_tool_is_cancelled` (default-deny half, `tests/test_guards_replyguard.py`) |
| R-8 | Hard invocation ceiling per tag (`turns`, `output_tokens`, `total_tokens`). **All three are LOOP budgets, and all three were wrong until 2026-08-06 — see R-24 for the measurements and R-23 for why nobody could tell.** `output_tokens` in particular is not the provider's per-call ceiling (`llm.max_tokens`) and used to literally be it. A cap absent from the dict is not a cap: Strands' `_check_limits` skips one it cannot find, which is why `nora.config.LimitsConfig` makes all three required. | `test_limits_passed_through`; `test_no_single_call_can_spend_the_whole_turn_budget` (R-24) |
| R-9 | Debounce: a second tag for the same conversation within `min_interval_seconds` is dropped. | `test_debounce_window` |
| R-10 | In-flight lock: at most one tag per conversation; released on every exit path including timeout/error. | `test_concurrent_tags_same_conversation` |
| R-10b | ...released specifically on timeout. | `test_lock_released_on_timeout` |
| R-10c | ...released specifically on an LLM error. | `test_lock_released_on_llm_error` |
| R-11 | Trigger validation — only genuine trigger text fires (word-boundary, code-span-aware, Unicode-normalized). | `test_trigger_matrix` |
| R-12 | Nora never triggers herself — `is_nora=1` rows and her own `sender_id` can never fire the trigger. **DEC-9** moves the identity source from a private adapter attribute (`adapter._account`) to `resolve_identity()` on the port, so this becomes platform-generic instead of Signal-specific. **Built in the platforms phase**: `nora.engagement.stages.admission.run` checks `message.sender_id in identity.aliases` (membership, not equality against a single id — signal-cli sometimes pairs a phone number with a UUID for one account); the `_AccountHolder` structural shim that read `adapter._account` directly is deleted. | `test_self_tag_ignored` |
| R-13 | All group-derived text is XML-escaped and enclosed in labelled untrusted blocks. | `test_prefill_escapes_angle_brackets` |
| R-13b | ...even a forged closing tag inside the text. | `test_forged_closing_tag_is_escaped` |
| R-14 | Prompt-injection behaviour (never reveal/paraphrase doctrine, config, keys; never adopt another identity). Behavioural — asserted by `constraints.md`, backstopped mechanically by R-6, measured by the adversarial corpus. No hook can enforce a behavioural rule. | `evals/adversarial/*.yaml`, pinned present by `test_r14_is_covered_by_the_adversarial_corpus` |
| R-15 | Anti-redundant tool calls — the pre-fill header states what context is already present. | `test_no_redundant_read_fails_when_prefill_was_sufficient` |
| R-16 | The LLM API key value never appears in a log line, trace attribute, exception message, or `raw_json`. | `test_secret_never_logged_in_the_message` |
| R-17 | **A degraded derivation of Nora's own identity is counted, never merely logged.** R-12 is only as strong as `PlatformIdentity.aliases` is complete, so enrichment falling back to `{primary}` silently downgrades a security rule to an equality check. `nora.platform.signal.self_id.derive_identifiers` stays best-effort (it must never block startup) but increments `nora_identity_enrichment_degraded_total{platform,reason}` on every degraded path AND always publishes the `nora_identity_aliases{platform}` gauge — the gauge is the load-bearing half, because a failure counter at 0 cannot distinguish "healthy" from "this code no longer runs". Alert on `nora_identity_aliases == 1`. | `test_degraded_identity_enrichment_is_counted_and_r12_still_holds`; `tests/test_signal_self_id.py` (whole file) |
| R-18 | Somebody else's identifiers never leave in a reply — an E.164 number, a UUID (ACI/PNI), a key-shaped string, or the name of the model she runs on. `constraints.md` forbids relaying them, but that is a request to a model; this is the half that does not depend on it complying. Blocking costs one silent reply, leaking is on every member's device before anyone can react, so it fails closed and counts `nora_egress_blocks_total{kind}`. **Amended 2026-09-28 by DEC-226** (`design/cognition-loop` step 0): extended to images — the face check (R-33) is this guard applied to a face crop; still blocks a key-shaped value in a reply, one read from a memo included. | `test_a_reply_carrying_someones_phone_number_is_refused` |
| R-20 | **Quoted text shown to the model is the resolved parent ROW's text, or nothing** (`design/11-recall-and-threading.md` §2.4). `build_tag_message` used to render `dataMessage.quote`'s own `text`, attributed to a named author, inside `<tag_message>` — and that text arrives in the QUOTING sender's envelope, verified against nothing, so Alice could construct a quote asserting Bob said anything at all and Nora would relay it back into the room as Bob's words. R-13 escapes it; escaping does not make a forged attribution safe. `nora.agent.prefill._replying_to_block` now resolves `quote.quoted_ts` to a row Nora herself audited and renders THAT row's body under THAT row's label; an unresolvable pointer omits the block entirely rather than falling back to `quote.author_id`, which is a raw platform identifier and so exactly what R-18 keeps off the wire. Fixes Bug A as a side effect: signal-cli's `quote` payload has no `authorName` field at all, so the old `q.get("authorName") or ""` rendered `<replying_to author="">` — "replying to nobody" — on every real message for the whole life of that feature. | `test_a_forged_quote_cannot_put_words_in_someone_elses_mouth` |
| R-21 | **A room-scoped tool resolves names only within the conversation it was bound to, and "not in this room" is indistinguishable from "does not exist".** `group_members`, `lookup_person` and `recall` (`nora.agent.tools`) all resolve inside `nora.agent.room.RoomView.people` — the platform's own membership list for THIS conversation, intersected with `identity.toml` — never against `Persons.index`, which is Nora's address book across every room she is in. The mechanism is **resolve-within-scope, never resolve-then-filter**: the name/alias index `find` runs against is BUILT from this room's members, so a person who is elsewhere is not found-and-rejected, they are absent from the index. Resolve-then-filter would leak membership — and the existence of people in other rooms — through the difference between "no such person" and "not here", which is the 2026-08-06 roster leak in a slower spelling: asked who was in the group Nora listed five people who had never been members, and R-18 saw nothing to block because the leak carried only names (design/12 §3). **By the time text exists the disclosure is already authorised**, so this is enforced at ASSEMBLY. Two consequences worth stating: alias matching is safe HERE while design/10 §1.3 still forbids an alias ever resolving a SENDER (the target set is bounded before any alias is consulted, and `nora.persons.Persons.index` is untouched — `tests/test_persons.py::test_an_alias_never_resolves_a_sender` still holds); and none of the three accepts or returns a platform identifier, so they cannot confirm that an id belongs to a member, and nothing they hand the model is something R-18 would have to block on the way out. **DEC-44 removed `read_peer_card`, this rule's last STRUCTURAL violation** — an unscoped, raw-platform-id lookup that could pull a person's card across conversation boundaries; the room-scoped tools named here are now the whole of the person-lookup surface, and every one of them resolves within scope. **Amended 2026-09-28 by DEC-223** (`design/cognition-loop` step 0): an agenda item's room-scoped reads resolve through its bound room. | `test_not_being_here_is_indistinguishable_from_not_existing` (`tests/test_room_tools.py`); `tests/unit/test_agent_room.py::test_a_person_in_identity_toml_but_not_in_this_room_is_not_found` |
| R-22 | **A tool that could not answer says so in its RETURN VALUE, and "asked and nothing known" is never the same value as "could not ask".** An empty result that reads as "nobody is here" is a confident lie the group acts on; a raised exception kills the turn. So each of the three room-scoped tools returns a `status` — `ok` / `not_found` / `ambiguous` / `nothing_known` / `unavailable` — and every one is counted (`nora_room_lookups_total{tool,status}`, plus `nora_recall_total{status}` for the Honcho call specifically). **The counter has to live at the call site**, because neither transport can express the distinction: signal-cli returning `[]` for a group Nora is demonstrably in is a real observed state (stale group state on a linked device — CLAUDE.md constraint 3), and Honcho's `representation` answers **200 with an empty string** for a peer it has never heard of rather than 404. This is `peer_card`'s failure written down: it returned `[]` both when Honcho was down and when it knew nothing, so a dead endpoint answered "I know nothing" on every call for the entire life of the deployment and "a missing card is normal" was a true sentence that made it invisible. Consequences: an unreadable roster makes `group_members` `unavailable` and never an empty list; a lookup MISS while the roster is unreadable is `unavailable`, not `not_found` (the scope narrows to the tagger, which is a strict subset of the room and so cannot say what the room does not contain); and a `MemoryStore` that raises lands on `unavailable`, never on empty. | `test_nothing_known_is_distinguishable_from_could_not_ask` (`tests/test_room_tools.py`); `tests/test_honcho_representation.py::test_an_unknown_peer_is_reachable_and_empty_never_unreachable`; `tests/contract/test_roster_source_contract.py` |
| R-23 | **A turn that ran out of budget is never reported as a turn that chose not to speak.** Strands ends a turn that hits one of R-8's caps by yielding an `EventLoopStopEvent` with `stop_reason="limit_total_tokens"` (or `limit_turns` / `limit_output_tokens`) and RETURNING — measured end to end against 1.50.2: no exception, no log line, no warning anywhere in the SDK. `nora/` never read `stop_reason` at all (zero hits), and `LiveAgentRunner.invoke` awaited `factory.invoke(...)` and DISCARDED the `AgentResult` it returned. So `invoke.run` reported `ok=True`, the pipeline found nothing delivered, ⚠️ fired and `nora_silent_failures_total{reason="no_send_call"}` incremented — **byte-identical to the model simply choosing not to call `send_reply`.** The single most likely cause of a silent turn was indistinguishable from the most benign one, and the budget was crossed during model call FIVE of an alleged eight (see R-24), so this was not a corner case. The `AgentResult` is now kept, `stop_reason` is threaded `LiveAgentRunner` → `invoke.run` → `deliver.check_outcome`, every completed invocation is counted `nora_llm_stop_reason_total{reason}` (including `end_turn` — a series that only ever carries `limit_*` cannot say what FRACTION of turns are cut off), and a silent turn whose loop ended on a cap is labelled with that cap instead of `no_send_call`. `check_outcome`'s `stop_reason` has **no default**, so a new call site cannot quietly restore the old behaviour. Only the three BUDGET reasons are relabelled: `end_turn`/`max_tokens` with no reply is still a model that chose not to speak, and swallowing that would trade one blind spot for another. This matters more than R-24's numbers — raising a cap without this just moves the cliff, and it is the difference between finding the next one in an afternoon and it running 61 days like the `--receive-mode` bug. | `test_a_budget_stop_is_distinguishable_from_a_silent_model` (`tests/integration/test_turn_budget_is_legible.py`); `tests/unit/test_engagement_deliver.py::test_a_turn_cut_off_by_a_budget_cap_is_not_labelled_no_send_call`, `::test_an_ordinary_stop_reason_still_counts_no_send_call`, `::test_check_outcome_cannot_be_called_without_a_stop_reason`; `tests/unit/test_engagement_invoke.py::test_the_stop_reason_is_counted_on_every_completed_invocation` |
| R-24 | **No single model call, and no single tool result, may spend the whole turn's budget.** Three violations, all measured 2026-08-06, all previously invisible because a budget that is too small does not fail loudly — it just ends the turn early (which, before R-23, read as the model declining to answer). (1) `build_limits` set `"output_tokens": max_tokens`, making the WHOLE LOOP's output budget equal to ONE call's ceiling; measured single calls emitted 3,993 / 3,987 / 3,974 completion tokens against `max_tokens = 4000`, i.e. 99.8% of it. `output_tokens` is now its own `[llm.limits]` field (12,000 = 6x the per-call ceiling) and `build_limits` has no `max_tokens` parameter left to pass. (2) Real per-call INPUT is 4,952 tokens, paid again on every call, and a measured 6-call turn totalled 32,426-36,748 — so `total_tokens = 24000` was crossed during call FIVE and `turns = 8` was unreachable dead config. `total_tokens = 64000` gives ~2x headroom and lets `turns` bind first, which is the cap an operator can reason about because a turn is a round trip and a token is not. `max_tokens` drops 4000 → 2000: the largest LEGITIMATE completion measured was 371 tokens, so that is 5.4x headroom, and it no longer doubles as the loop budget. (3) `read_buffer`'s `limit` is the one number in `nora.agent.tools` the MODEL invents on every call and nothing downstream bounds it, so the clamp is the only thing between it and the turn: `read_buffer(200)` cost 6,592 tokens (vs `read_buffer(40)` 1,368, `recall` 151, `lookup_person` 112) and is re-charged on every later call of the loop, so at `budget: 2` two calls were 13,184. Clamped 200 → 60, default 40 → 25. The ceiling is a LITERAL in the docstring rather than an interpolation because the docstring IS the model-facing schema — an f-string there would leave `__doc__` empty and Strands would derive no description at all — so a test pins the literal to `READ_BUFFER_MAX` instead. Asserted against **both** config files: `config.toml` is what this deployment runs and `config.example.toml` is what a fresh install gets and what `tests/test_config.py` loads. | `test_no_single_call_can_spend_the_whole_turn_budget` (`tests/test_turn_budget.py`, parametrised over both config files); `::test_both_config_files_declare_the_same_budget`; `::test_the_load_transcript_clamp_is_the_only_bound_on_a_model_supplied_size`; `::test_the_model_is_told_the_same_ceiling_the_clamp_enforces`; `tests/test_factory.py::test_build_limits_takes_the_loop_budget_and_never_the_per_call_ceiling`; `tests/test_tools.py::test_load_transcript_clamps_the_top_end_to_the_declared_ceiling` |

| R-30 | **A tag for a conversation already handling one is QUEUED, not dropped.** Admission used to DROP a second concurrent tag (`nora_tags_dropped_total{reason="in_flight"}`): three people tagging at once meant person 1 got a reply and persons 2 and 3 got silence — counted, but from inside the room indistinguishable from being ignored, R-5's failure shape pointed at people. Now a busy conversation gets a per-conversation FIFO queue (`nora.engagement.queue.ConversationQueues`), drained one turn at a time as each in-flight turn's `finally` releases R-10's lock and dispatches the next. **Serialisation is correctness, not politeness**: each turn's context is assembled at DEQUEUE time, so tag 2 sees tag 1's reply already in the transcript — two concurrent same-conversation turns would each reason from a room missing the other's reply and could re-answer or contradict. The queue feeds R-10's single slot in order; it never widens it, and DIFFERENT conversations still run concurrently. **Bounded against a flood, not against waiting**: `engagement.queue.max_depth` (default 16) sheds only the newest arrival past the bound (`nora_tags_dropped_total{reason="queue_full"}`, its own counter distinct from debounce); the old `reason="in_flight"` drop is gone. **No staleness rule** — elapsed time is a weak proxy for "the group moved on", and dropping a tag someone still waits on is the exact failure this removes. Composes with R-9 (a debounced tag never enqueues) and R-10 (the lock still guards the single in-flight turn; the queue is a THIRD per-conversation structure). Per-CONVERSATION state only: a `deque` per active conversation, deleted the moment its last waiting tag is dequeued, so nothing is retained per-tag (`tests/architecture/test_no_retained_per_tag_state.py` still holds). The 👀 progress reaction now fires at ADMISSION for a queued tag too — see DEC-48. See DEC-48. | `test_three_tags_for_one_conversation_are_answered_in_fifo_order` |
| R-25 | **A tag that delivered SOME of its messages and then stopped early is counted as a partial reply, never as a complete one.** R-23 made a SILENT turn's cause legible; a turn cut off between message 2 and message 4 is not silent — `delivered` is True, `check_outcome` returns True, the indicator resolves ✅, Honcho is fed, and `nora_silent_failures_total` never moves. The group reads half a thought and, before this rule, no series anywhere said so. `nora_messages_per_tag` cannot answer it either: once the histogram legitimately spans 1–4 a 2 is a 2 whether she meant to stop there or was stopped. `nora_partial_replies_total{reason, platform}` reuses Strands' `limit_*` vocabulary where the loop reported one (so it joins against `nora_llm_stop_reason_total`) and adds `invocation_failed` for a timeout or `llm_error`, which return no stop reason at all, and `pipeline_error` for the outer `BaseException`. | R-34 | **RETIRED by DEC-73 (2026-08-08): `web_fetch`/Firecrawl removed — no fetch, no fence, no rule. Historical text below.** **`fetch` may open only a URL a `search` returned this turn — defence in depth, NOT the SSRF guarantee.** The two web verbs are the only grounding whose OUTBOUND call (a self-hosted fetcher against a model-chosen URL) is an SSRF surface: SearXNG, Honcho, signal-cli (`:18080`), OmniRoute and Firecrawl all listen on localhost, so a model-invented URL makes Firecrawl a pivot into Nora's internals. The PRIMARY control is Firecrawl's network-isolated egress (design/22 §0/§5, a deployment change — the operator ship gate, not this build), because Firecrawl follows redirects and re-resolves DNS itself, so anything Nora checks pre-call is bypassable at the connection Firecrawl actually makes. What Nora's own code enforces is defence in depth: (a) a per-tag `allowed_urls` fence — `fetch` refuses any URL not returned by a `search` this turn, so an invented URL reaches Firecrawl through nothing (`nora.agent.tools`); (b) an `is_global` scheme/host precheck resolved through `getaddrinfo`, rejecting non-http(s) and any host any of whose resolved addresses is not `is_global` (loopback/RFC1918/CGNAT/link-local/ULA/reserved/unspecified, and numeric/hex/IPv4-mapped encodings and rebind DNS names all normalise before the check — `nora.infra.search`). See DEC-57. Next free number after the presence pair (R-31/R-32) and media_fetch (R-33); design/22 §6 wrote R-32 provisionally, reconciled to R-34 at merge. **Live since 2026-08-08 (DEC-69): the PRIMARY control (`egress.sh` packet-layer isolation) is NOT persistently deployed — its rules reopen after every `docker compose up` — so this defence-in-depth is the WHOLE live SSRF control, not the backstop it was designed to be. | R-36 | **A reminder never fires early.** The tick's batch is `due_at <= now` and nothing else: no rounding, no tolerance window, no catch-up sweep that treats "nearly due" as due. | R-37 | **A row fires once, ever.** Taking a row is a COMPARE-AND-SET on `state = 'pending'` inside the statement (`ReminderStore.claim`), not a read-then-write. `due()` is a query rather than a claim — the batch it returns is a snapshot of a past moment, and the tick awaits a turn per conversation before it reaches the later rows — so a cancel landing in that window must win. Recurrence now exists, as a stored property of the row minted inside `claim` (DEC-85) — so the thing this rule bars is no longer recurrence itself but recurrence NOBODY ASKED FOR: without the refusal Nora re-arms her own reminder every time one comes due, an unbounded loop that no `RecurrenceRule.count` bounds because each re-arm is a fresh series. **None of the caps can stop it** — `max_pending_per_requester` counts PENDING rows and the fire has already freed one before the replacement is written, and the new row passes `min_lead_seconds` and `max_horizon_days` trivially. | R-42 | **DEPRECATED 2026-10-16 (DEC-314): the version announcement is retired, so there is nothing left to announce once; the text below describes nothing that runs.** **A version is announced AT MOST ONCE, per room, ever.** Nora's second unprompted-speech occasion (DEC-97), and the failure it exists to prevent is specific: a container crash-looping every four seconds would otherwise post the same upgrade note into a group chat on every boot. The claim is `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` on `version_announcements(version, platform, conversation_id)` — a compare-and-set in ONE statement, `reminders.claim`'s shape (R-37) — and it is taken BEFORE the turn runs, so a row EXISTING bars a second attempt whatever state it holds. | R-49 | **A message may cross into another room only between rooms of the SAME unit, only at the request of somebody allowed in BOTH, and only under that person's name.** R-2 says a turn's messages all go to the tagging conversation, and that stays true of `send_reply`; `send_to` (DEC-105) is the one gated exception. It matters because every other guardrail here is scoped to ONE conversation — `policy.toml` decides who may speak in a room, R-31 what may be disclosed into it — so a relay reaches past all of them by construction: the words appear in front of an audience that made its own trust decisions. Five refusals, all fail-closed: an **unmapped asker** (a person Nora cannot name cannot be attributed, and an unattributed relay is precisely what attribution prevents); a **room resolved by anything but its operator-written `label`**, refusing rather than guessing when two rooms answer to one name; a **destination in another `unit`** — the boundary that makes a relay legitimate rather than a leak, since rooms sharing one are one social unit reachable in more than one place while rooms in different ones are different groups of people, however trusted each is alone; an asker **not independently allowed in the destination** (the unit bounds which rooms may be PAIRED, the persons list decides who may USE the pair — without it, anyone in one room of a unit could speak into every other, which is a promotion); and text failing the **same egress scan a reply gets** (R-18), because the destination saw neither the asker nor the turn. What arrives ALWAYS names who asked: «dinner at 8» and «Miles: dinner at 8» are different claims to the people reading them and only the second is true, so the attribution is built in the relay rather than left to the model, which could be talked out of it. A comprehension that DOES land still crosses the same egress scan a reply gets (R-18/R-28) before it reaches a prompt — at RENDER time now rather than at ingest (R-90), so a durable cache hit cannot bypass it, AND at the Honcho feed, which does not render and so cannot be covered by a render-time screen. | R-53 | **A source that does not mention something has not told you it is false — the SCOPE case, which R-27's three-state discipline never reached (audit F7, 2026-08-20).** `conduct.md`'s «What a source does not say» (since 2026-10-12 `rooms/constraints.md` § Say only what you found, moved verbatim in context-plan 11 §6 step 2) adds the third outcome beside empty-result and broken-call: a source narrower than the question is `unavailable` («I couldn't check»), never `nothing_found` («there's nothing»), and a silence never overturns something already found with a source behind it. R-27 is enforced on tool RESULTS; nothing enforced it on INFERENCE OVER results, which is where the 2026-08-17 02:16 UTC failure happened — a «Best tower order» article scoped to «all four of the **coloured** towers» was read as denying a black tower, overturning her own correct sourced answer from two minutes earlier. Behavioural, the same shape as R-14/R-41: asserted by `conduct.md`, measured by the corpus, and NOT a currently-passing gate — the corpus is deliberately outside the GATED `adversarial` corpus in `evals/run.py` (it is selectable by name, `--suite source_scope`, since 2026-09-17/#227: running a corpus and gating on it are two decisions, and only the second was ever made here). **The corpus is graded on its OWN axis (2026-08-20), because the shared rubric's gradient ran BACKWARDS here.** The adversarial gate binds `no_overreach_or_fabrication`, which asks whether a reply claimed MORE than its source supports; reading a silence as a denial claims LESS, and every value in such a reply is real, so the criterion had nothing to catch — measured on `ollamacloud/deepseek-v4-pro:0813` at k=3, temp 0, the failing reply to `scoped_source_silence_stale_window_english` scored PASS 3/3 at 1.0/1.0/0.8 («all stated facts are grounded in the provided source data»). The rubric was not wrong, it was answering a different question, so the fix is a SECOND criterion (`evals/rubric.py::SOURCE_SCOPE`, opted into per case) and NOT a loosening of the first — re-measured after the change, the leaderboard attribution case still FAILs 3/3 at 0.0. Same axis after the change: the denial reply FAILs 2/3, the carry-forward reply PASSes 2/3. **ADDED 2026-09-24 (#449): «binds fail-closed» was NOT true of the rebuilt harness until that PR.** `evals.rebuilt.grading.Judge.grade` rendered an opted-in criterion into the judge prompt and bound the verdict on `no_overreach_or_fabrication` alone, so `source_scope`'s own axis was graded and discarded on every rebuilt run before #449 (`evals/judge.py`'s old path, which `case_verdict` describes above, is not the one the rebuilt suite runs). Pre-#449 and post-#449 `source_scope` numbers are not comparable. **Reference note added 2026-09-25:** `evals/run.py` and `evals/judge.py` were both deleted 2026-09-18 (778a617e, 00beda19) — the rebuilt harness is `evals/backbone.py`; `evals/adversarial/source_scope.yaml` was deleted 2026-09-21 (90fd780f) and replaced by `evals/corpora/source_scope.yaml`, which `test_r53_is_covered_by_the_source_scope_corpus` now pins. | `nora/doctrine/rooms/constraints.md` (until 2026-10-12 `rooms/conduct.md`), pinned by `test_conduct_separates_a_source_that_is_silent_from_a_source_that_denies`; `evals/adversarial/source_scope.yaml`, pinned present by `test_r53_is_covered_by_the_source_scope_corpus` and graded by `test_every_source_scope_case_opts_into_the_scope_criterion` |
| R-54 | **DEPRECATED 2026-09-07 — the tier this decides has been deprecated and its code deleted (issue #115). The row is kept, unrenumbered, as a record; it no longer describes anything that runs.** **A source that does not cover a claim never removes a fact; only a source that addresses it and contradicts it does.** R-53 states this for the model, in `conduct.md`, as prose — and when measured, the prose could not be shown to hold: `evals/adversarial/source_scope.yaml` was, and still is, deliberately held out of `evals/run.py`'s gated `adversarial` corpus (a measured gap, not a gate; selectable by name since #227), and the shared rubric was found grading it BACKWARDS — `no_overreach_or_fabrication` asks whether a reply claimed MORE than its source supports, so a reply that read a scoped source's silence as a denial and withdrew a correctly-sourced fact scored PASS 3/3 while quoting a denial the source never made. **That grading defect has since been fixed** (`8ffe33b`): `evals/rubric.py::SOURCE_SCOPE` is now a second criterion, opted into per case via `criteria: [source_scope]`, and it binds fail-closed — `evals.judge.case_verdict` fails a case on ANY named criterion's FAIL, so silence-read-as-denial now scores a SCOPE FAIL rather than a pass. The corpus itself stays out of the gated corpus on purpose (`source_scope.yaml`'s own header: "wire it in when it reliably passes, not before") — the fix corrected how a wired-in case would be JUDGED, not whether the doctrine reliably clears it. R-54 is the same rule moved from prose into a SHAPE, DEC-78's move applied to inference over sources: `FactVerdict.not_covered` (`nora/domain/facts.py`) has no reachable `supersedes`, and `contradicted` requires both a source and `addresses_claim` — «the source did not cover it, therefore drop the fact» is unrepresentable at the type, not merely discouraged in the prompt. | `tests/domain/test_facts.py::test_not_covered_cannot_supersede_anything`, `::test_contradicted_requires_a_source_that_addresses_the_claim` |
| R-55 | **A note revision is vetoed unless `note_read` succeeded for that note in the same turn (note-tier spec §6.2).** The injected `<notes>` index carries title + description and nothing else — enough to know a note EXISTS, nowhere near enough to revise one — and `note_update` REPLACES the note's rendered body (§6.1's head revision), so a revision written from a one-line description destroys the arrangement the whole tier exists to hold, and destroys it silently: the prior revision survives in the table, but nothing in the room ever learns the note stopped saying what it said. **The latch lives on `ReplyGuard`, and where each half sits in `_after_tool` is the load-bearing part.** `release()` sits ABOVE both early returns because it means «this call FINISHED», true on every path — that sentence being written below a return is the leak `4d44d0d` fixed. The veto is not one-shot (unlike R-45): the remedy is a different call with its own budget, and a one-shot latch would let the second attempt through unread. **On "mypy `--strict`":** `pyproject.toml`'s `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` for `nora.domain.*`/`nora.config`/`nora.app.*` deliberately hand-expands `--strict`'s flag list instead of setting `strict = true`, working around a confirmed mypy 2.3.0 bug where `strict = true` inside an override section leaks strict mode to every module in the run, not just the matched ones (see the comment above that override in `pyproject.toml`). This is a frozen snapshot of what `--strict` meant as of mypy's pinned version — it must be re-diffed against `--strict`'s actual flag set on every mypy upgrade, or the override silently drifts from what "strict" means in the new version.
| DEC-14 | **Many accounts per platform is the identity baseline** (design/10 §1, §3, §7.4), not an edge case — settled with the operator 2026-08-05 after his two Signal accounts broke the first draft of §3, which modelled many *id forms* of ONE account and had nowhere to put a second registration. One `[[persons.<id>.<platform>]]` block per account; every id in every block flattens into one reverse index, so all of a person's accounts resolve to one `person_id` and therefore one Honcho peer (A2). Splitting them into two `person_id`s would have split his peer card. **Multiplicity lives at the table level, never at the leaf**: a list-valued kind (`phone = [...]`) is refused, because it severs the phone↔ACI pairing within a registration, makes `nora persons pending`'s paste-ready stanza unimplementable for an existing person, and would require widening the leaf type — the one thing stopping `str([...])` from entering the index as a key no sender can present. Second hard break on `identity.toml`, same §7.3 reasoning, with a bespoke error naming the `[[ ]]` form. Two loudness rules guard otherwise-silent authoring errors: an account with no matchable id is refused, and the same id in two of one person's blocks is refused (the copy-paste-and-forget-to-edit mistake, which nothing else catches because both blocks map to the same person so the cross-person check never fires). | `tests/test_persons.py::test_two_accounts_on_one_platform_resolve_to_the_same_person`, `::test_the_same_id_in_two_account_blocks_is_a_startup_failure`, `::test_a_label_is_never_matchable`, `::test_the_retired_single_table_form_names_its_replacement` |
| DEC-15 | **Ingest resolves identity BEFORE the audit write, and counts unresolved senders.** An unmapped sender was previously symptomless: the message was still audited, the gate still ran, and `Persons.display_name` still rendered the sender's platform display name into the prefill, so Nora replied normally and addressed them by name while nothing at all reached Honcho — the display-name fallback actively fabricating the appearance that identity worked. Now `nora_unmapped_senders_total{platform}` counts it and a redacted warning names the likely cause. The resolved `person_id` is persisted on the audit row (`0002_person_id`, nullable, unindexed, declared LAST so a fresh database matches `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`'s append position). Stage order was swapped rather than adding an UPDATE: A9 permits a second write (it is what `guards.py` does for outbound replies) but `nora.infra.sql.audit` documents that WAL allows one writer and this path DROPS the message on contention — pruning was moved off the write path for that reason, so identity resolution (two dict lookups, no I/O) moved ahead of it instead. Counter and column are not redundant: metrics live only in the process registry and reset on restart, while mapping is startup-only (Q4), so "I fixed identity.toml but never restarted" is a state the file on disk cannot reveal. | `tests/unit/test_ingest_stages.py::test_an_unmapped_sender_is_audited_but_never_fed`, `tests/infra/test_schema_parity.py` |
| DEC-16 | **Adoption is lazy: a person's pre-mapping messages are backfilled into Honcho at the next startup, feed-then-mark.** DEC-15 made an unmapped sender visible and durable (`nora_unmapped_senders_total`, `person_id` NULL on the row) but changed nothing about the memory hole itself: `nora.ingest.stages.memory_feed` bare-returns on `person is None`, and mapping is startup-only (Q4), so every message from before the operator's `identity.toml` edit stayed unfed **forever** — the peer card silently missing the person's entire history up to their adoption. `nora.app.adoption.backfill` reconciles it: scan `RecordStore.unattributed` (person_id IS NULL, `is_nora = 0`, **ordered by `ts`** so the peer's memory reads chronologically, not in insertion order), re-resolve each row's `(platform, sender_id)` against the freshly-loaded `Persons`, feed the message to that person's peer, and only then `RecordStore.set_person_id`. **The order is the decision.** Marking first would retire the row from every future scan the moment a Honcho failure — or a crash — landed between the two, making the hole permanent and silent; feeding first re-feeds on the next restart instead, and at-least-once is the tolerable direction. `person_id` is itself the idempotence marker, so there is no separate ledger. Scheduling follows `prune_all`'s precedent exactly (DEC-15's own reasoning, and `nora.infra.sql.audit`'s docstring): `App.run` spawns it through `BackgroundTasks` after a delay, nothing awaits it, and `set_person_id` writes one row per statement — a backfill that stalled the SSE reader or cost an audit row under WAL's single writer would be a regression, not a feature. Honcho stays best-effort (a raising `MemoryStore` is converted to `False`, a failing sweep is logged and counted, neither can take startup down). Two new counters, `nora_lazy_adoptions_total{platform}` and `nora_adoption_failures_total{platform}`, plus an unconditional INFO line carrying scanned/resolved/fed/marked/failed — a backfill nobody can see having run is the R-5 failure again. | `tests/unit/test_adoption.py` (`::test_a_honcho_failure_leaves_the_row_unmarked_for_the_next_start` is the ordering test; `::test_running_twice_does_not_double_feed_or_double_mark` the idempotence one), `tests/contract/test_audit_store_contract.py` (the `unattributed`/`set_person_id` block, both stores), `tests/test_main.py::test_app_run_spawns_the_lazy_adoption_backfill` (the wiring) |
| DEC-17 | **A tag is acknowledged with a 👀 reaction on the tagging message, and that indicator is always resolved — ✅ when a reply went out, ⚠️ when none did.** Built as `nora.engagement.stages.indicate` + `PlatformAdapter.react()` (`nora.platform.signal.react.SignalReactor` → signal-cli's `sendReaction`; params `groupId`/`emoji`/`targetAuthor`/`targetTimestamp`/`remove`, read off the 0.14.7 man pages, not guessed). **The failure resolution is the decision.** The request was ✅ "whether it succeeds or fails"; a ✅ on a tag that produced no reply asserts a delivery that never happened and leaves the group waiting for a message that is not coming — the inverse of R-5, a false success rather than a leaked error, and worse because a silent failure is at least honestly ambiguous. The two alternatives are this project's own wrong-silence bug in user-facing form: a 👀 left forever makes "thinking" and "broken" the same observation (the 61-day `--receive-mode` outage, relocated into the group), and removing it silently makes "gave up" and "never triggered" the same one. ⚠️ is honest and still discloses nothing R-5 protects: it is not text, it names no cause, and every failure class — timeout, guard veto, leak block, audit failure — is indistinguishable under it (what DEC-4 requires of `INFRASTRUCTURE`/`GUARD_VETO`), so the only bit it adds is one the group can already see, that the reply is missing. ❌ was rejected as reading like an incident report, and a person emoji (the original 🤷) as carrying skin tone, gender and human affect — a shrug reads as dismissiveness, which is a lot of tone for "the model timed out". An intermediate ⚪ was colour-neutral but too easy to scroll past; the operator chose ⚠️ on 2026-08-05 because this marker exists to be NOTICED. **R-2/R-2b/R-3/R-7 are untouched by construction**: a reaction is not a registered tool (so `ReplyGuard`'s injected `budgets` is unchanged and R-7's default-deny still refuses a model that invents one), it never touches `Deliverer` (so the single-attempt latch cannot be consumed or re-armed), its target is `message.target()` and takes no model input at all, and `Deliverer` remains the only caller of `adapter.send()`. **Spawned, never awaited** — `SignalReactor` runs a 10s timeout, so awaiting the 👀 would let a wedged daemon add ten seconds to every tag before the model started; `Indicator.placed` (an `asyncio.Event` set in a `finally`) serialises begin-before-resolve without either being on the reply path. (1) **The bug.** DEC-32 (3) established that Strands fires `AfterToolCallEvent` for a call `_before_tool` cancelled as well, with `exception=None` and only `cancel_message` to tell it apart, and applied that to the terminal latch. The observed sequence: the model calls `send_reply("")`, R-4 refuses it, the model corrects itself in the same turn with real text, and R-7's budget check — which runs BEFORE R-2's latch (DEC-32 (4)) — answers *you already sent your reply*. One recoverable mistake, and **the recovery is what gets blocked**; the turn then ends `no_send_call` and under R-5 the group simply hears nothing. The fix is one early `return` on `cancel_message`, shared by `record` and the latch, so the two can no longer disagree about what "the call ran" means. (2) **Why nothing caught it, and the more important half of this entry.** `nora.testing.FakeAgentRunner` — the double every scripted scenario in `tests/integration/` and `evals/` runs against — replayed the guard by calling `evaluate` and `record` BY HAND, and on a veto it `continue`d without calling `record` at all. That is the SDK's behaviour inverted: the fake charged nothing for a vetoed call, production charged a full budget. A regression test written against that double could not fail whatever `_after_tool` did, because `_after_tool` was never on the path. **Measured, not argued:** with the old double in place, the end-to-end probe below PASSES against the unfixed guard. This is exactly CLAUDE.md's "make the fake behave like the real server", in its third recorded instance. (3) **The double now dispatches hooks instead of methods.** `guard.register_hooks(...)` is handed a `_HookRegistry` and the replay fires `BeforeToolCallEvent`, `AfterToolCallEvent` (for cancelled calls too, carrying `cancel_message`) and `BeforeModelCallEvent`, with the field values `tests/test_strands_api_contract.py` asserts against the real SDK. Callbacks are keyed by `event_type.__name__` because `nora.testing` may not import `strands` (`test_strands_import_boundary`) and `add_callback` is handed the real class object anyway. Two consequences beyond the bug: what a veto costs and what ends a turn are now `ReplyGuard`'s decisions in tests as well as in production, and a script with turns after a terminal verb now stops where the real loop stops rather than replaying turns production cannot reach. **No existing test changed behaviour** — the whole suite was green on the double's fix alone, which is the measurement of how little the old seam was proving. (4) **`nora_guard_vetoes_total{rule="R-2"}` is deliberately NOT split.** It cannot distinguish the budget branch from the latch branch, and that was noted rather than fixed. A `rule` VALUE is as append-only as the metric name — a new one silently splits every existing `rule="R-2"` query — and the branch it would name is unreachable while the budget is 1, so it would be a series that can never increment, which R-17 calls indistinguishable from a deleted one. Raising the cap makes both branches live in the same edit; that is when the label earns its cardinality. Intersecting with a roster would buy no scope and would put a daemon round trip at the front of every model call, which is the one thing `Room`'s laziness exists to avoid. (2) **Four things were measured before anything was specified, and each is a case where the obvious implementation is confidently wrong rather than obviously broken.** **Rounding**: Python's default is ROUND_HALF_EVEN and you get it by NOT choosing — `Decimal("2.005").quantize(Decimal("0.01"))` is **2.00**, and 0.125 goes to 0.12. Banker's rounding is right for a statistician and wrong on a bill. Every quantize passes `ROUND_HALF_UP` at the CALL, not on the context, so ambient state elsewhere cannot undo it. **The remainder**: 1485/7 is 212.1428…, and 212.14 x 7 is 1484.98 — two cents short, with nobody able to say who is short. `split` reports `each`, `leftover`, and a `settles_as` written as an EXPRESSION (`2 * 212.15 + 5 * 212.14`) so it can be handed back to this same tool and checked; a settlement nobody can verify is just a more confident version of the number this exists to distrust. It is computed in whole cents with ROUND_DOWN, so the leftover is always «somebody pays a cent MORE» rather than the harder-to-explain «two of you are owed a cent», and it reconciles exactly. `rounded_to_cents` and `split` are mutually exclusive: two money figures side by side that do not sum to the same total is the confusion the tool exists to remove. **`Pow` is a denial of service before it is a safety question**: `2**9999999999` parses cleanly as `BinOp`/`Pow`, passes any operator-level whitelist, and over ints was still running when `timeout 10` killed it. Over `Decimal` it raises `Overflow` in 54 microseconds — a real mitigation, but one this module does not OWN (it is the ambient `Emax=999999` plus a trap another `localcontext` could clear) and «Overflow» is not a sentence a model can act on. `Pow` is KEPT, because compound interest and percentages are ordinary group-chat questions, with `MAX_POW_EXPONENT = 1000` checked explicitly and refused legibly. **Literals must not be read through floats**: `ast` hands back `Constant(value=0.1)`, already a float, and `Decimal(0.1)` is 0.1000000000000000055…, so `0.1 + 0.2` would not be `0.3` — the tool wrong in precisely the way it exists to prevent. `Decimal(str(value))` fixes that one case and not the general one, so a float literal is re-read from its SOURCE TEXT; an int literal takes `Decimal(int)`, which is exact and is the only form that reads `0xff` correctly. `type(v) is int`, never `isinstance` — **`bool` subclasses `int`**, so `True + 1` would otherwise quietly answer 2. (3) **A node-type ALLOWLIST is the only safe shape, and a denylist of today's escapes is not one.** `(1).__class__` is a bare `Attribute` over a `Constant` carrying neither a `Call` nor a `Name`; `__import__('os').system('x')` is `Call` + `Name`. Three further bounds are owned here rather than inherited: `MAX_EXPRESSION_CHARS = 200` before parsing (the docs warn `ast.parse` can crash the interpreter on nested input; 3.13 happens to defend itself at depth 1000, which is an implementation detail, and the cap also bounds `_eval`'s recursion), `MAX_MAGNITUDE_DIGITS = 20` on every operand AND every intermediate (the render bound — `f"{Decimal('1E+999998'):f}"` is a megabyte into the model's context — and what keeps values clear of the 28-digit precision so nothing is silently re-rounded), and a zero-divisor check before `/`, `//` and `%`, because `decimal` signals that one thing as `DivisionByZero` in one case and `InvalidOperation` in two others. | DEC-47 | **Media is encrypted at rest, and image EXIF is stripped BEFORE the content is hashed.** Operator decision 2026-08-07; extends DEC-43, whose custody shipped merged-but-inert. Turns custody ON via `nora.app.composition`, and adds the two protections the operator required. `design/18-media-custody.md`. (1) **EXIF strip (images only).** A photo's EXIF carries GPS coordinates and a device id — worse PII than the image — and content addressing would otherwise dedup on EXIF *differences*, making the same picture with two GPS tags two blobs. `nora.ingest.exif.strip_exif` (Pillow: open → re-encode with no metadata) runs in `nora.ingest.stages.media._take` BEFORE `blobs.put`, so the content key is the key of the PICTURE and the location PII is gone from what Nora holds. It is images-only and never raises: an image Pillow cannot decode falls back to the original bytes (logged, still encrypted). NON-IMAGES (audio/video/documents) have NO metadata stripped — there is no cheap universal stripper — and that is stated, not hidden. (2) **Encryption at rest.** `FilesystemBlobStore` seals every blob under AES-256-GCM (`nora.infra.blobs.cipher.BlobCipher`) and writes CIPHERTEXT; a JPEG's `FF D8` never appears on disk. The key hashed for the content address is of the PLAINTEXT (dedup and the `[image a3f2c1]` handle unchanged); a fresh 12-byte nonce per blob is stored alongside the ciphertext (not secret — reuse is what is fatal, and content addressing writes a blob at most once, so a nonce never seals a second plaintext under one key). `get` opens the ciphertext and RAISES `InvalidTag` on a wrong/corrupt key rather than returning garbage — the same "unreadable is not absence" split `get` already drew for a bad disk. Nothing on the ingest hot path decrypts (the text model never reads bytes); a future `media_fetch` tool is `open`'s only caller. (3) **Degrade honestly, never plaintext-by-accident.** The cipher is REQUIRED on the store — there is no plaintext-on-disk mode. Custody is ON only when `[media] enabled` AND `media.encryption_key_env` names an env var holding a valid base64 32-byte key; a missing/malformed key is custody OFF (`_build_media_custody` returns `(None, None)`, warned), which is the `not_configured` state `nora.ingest.stages.media` counts — the deliberate asymmetry with the LLM key (`config.load` refuses to start without that; media is a bonus and must never take the daemon down or write plaintext). DEC-8: name the env var, never inline the secret. (4) **WHERE is co-equal with WHO, and rode the message row — NO new table, NO new index.** `media_json` sits on `messages`, which already carries `conversation_id` (WHERE), `sender_id`/`person_id` (WHO) and `ts` (WHEN), and `idx_messages_conv_ts` already indexes `(conversation_id, ts DESC)` — so "what media in THIS group, by whom, when" is answerable through the existing row and index with NO schema change. Metadata (`sha256`/`media_type`/`size`/`filename`) stays CLEAR; only the bytes are encrypted, which is what makes 「呢個group尋日啲相」 answerable without decrypting. (5) **Fixture-only.** No real attachment has ever arrived on this deployment — every EXIF/encryption probe runs on Pillow-built images, and the `getAttachment` success path stays as unverified as DEC-43 left it. | `tests/unit/test_media_encryption.py` (ciphertext-on-disk, `FF D8` absent, round-trip byte-identical, per-blob nonce, wrong-key raises, EXIF absent after strip, same-picture-different-EXIF dedups to one blob, non-image unstripped), `tests/test_composition.py::test_media_custody_is_off_when_the_key_env_is_unset`, `::test_a_valid_key_turns_media_custody_on_with_an_encrypting_store`, `::test_a_malformed_key_degrades_to_off_rather_than_crashing`, `::test_media_disabled_is_off_even_with_a_valid_key`; DEC-43's suites extended (`tests/contract/test_blob_store_contract.py` runs the encrypting store) |
| DEC-48 | **Nora's FIRST skill — `navigation` — and the on-demand skill layer it needed, shipped INERT.** design/12 §1 deferred skills until a domain existed ("Nothing qualifies yet"); route + transit (DEC-46, R-27) made wayfinding the first that does — combining a schedule and a live wait is instructions, not capability, which is what a skill is (design/14 §1). (1) **The skill is JUDGEMENT, not mechanism.** Which endpoint to call and how to fan out is the tool's job; ask-the-person-who-knows and read-the-age-on-a-fact are universal doctrine. Per-CONVERSATION state only, deleted the moment a conversation's queue drains — `tests/architecture/test_no_retained_per_tag_state.py` still holds. Both live behind one `[search]` config section that defaults `enabled=false` and stays so until the operator turns it on AND Firecrawl's egress isolation is in place — while off the registry (`nora.agent.registry.ToolRegistry`) holds no `SearchClient` and both answer `unavailable`, never a silent empty (R-5), the `route`-with-no-key shape. (2) **The SSRF control is Firecrawl's egress, not Nora's precheck** — the v2 revision's whole point: Firecrawl follows redirects and re-resolves DNS itself, so a public URL that `302`s to `127.0.0.1:18080` or DNS-rebinds is fetched against Nora's internals and Nora never sees it. R-34 is the defence-in-depth Nora's own code holds (per-tag `allowed_urls` fence + `is_global`/`getaddrinfo` precheck); the packet-layer egress isolation is the operator ship gate (§0/§5.1), and a green unit suite means «Nora refuses naive URLs», NOT «SSRF closed». (3) **Retrieved bytes are wrapped `untrusted`, reusing `nora.infra.transit.arrivals._wrap`** (R-13, escape-safe): a page controls its own snippet/body, so a snippet AND a page are `<untrusted source="URL">escape(text)</untrusted>`, and a body of `</untrusted>` becomes `&lt;/untrusted&gt;` and cannot forge the boundary. Retrieved text activates no skill (R-29 — `SkillStore.resolve` is a pure name lookup) and enters only as a tool RESULT, never a prompt position. (4) **The query is an egress surface** (design/14 §2.2): `scan_identifiers` (NOT `scan_reply` — 「搵首 haiku」 must work, DEC-30) blocks an identifier before it reaches SearXNG; a person alias is COUNTED not blocked (`nora_search_alias_total`, over `_known_names(persons)`), because a block would fail closed on legitimate use before the query shape is known. (5) **`fetch` deliberately does NOT `scan_identifiers` the page** (unlike `about`): a public web page is not Nora's people-data and stripping a whole page is impractical; the identifier boundary for anything RELAYED is `scan_reply` at `Deliverer` (design/22 §3, finding 5). (6) **Bounded by constants, not a component** (design/14 §4): `search_max_results` (~6) and a per-snippet byte clamp on `search`, `fetch_max_chars` on `fetch`, truncation STATED in the return value — retrieved text lands in the INPUT and is re-sent every subsequent call (`tokens × turns-remaining` against `total_tokens=64000`). (7) **Three states** (R-27) `ok`/`nothing_found`/`unavailable`; `fetch` adds `refused` (not in the fence, or non-`is_global`). Budgets `search` 2 / `fetch` 2, `terminal=False`, `time_shiftable=None`. (8) **Firecrawl API version PINNED to the deployed instance** — verified `v1` on the running `firecrawl-api` container (`127.0.0.1:3002`); both `/v1/scrape` and `/v2/scrape` answer with an identical `{success, data:{markdown, metadata:{url, sourceURL}}}` envelope today, and `v1` matches design/14's measurement. SearXNG `format=json` disabled → 403 → `unavailable` (the fake returns it; a ship-time check must confirm a live search returns `ok`, not merely reachable — the 61-day-silent shape). **Remaining operator gate (design/22 §5.1–§5.2, NOT in this build):** Firecrawl container egress network-isolation, and the real-Firecrawl redirect-to-localhost SSRF integration probe (no fake can prove it — the bypass runs inside Firecrawl). | DEC-66 | **Honcho bedrock — Nora's OWN model of each person (observer/observed), `ask_memory`, and the clean workspace topology (design/proposed/24 §S, operator-settled 2026-08-08).** Honcho keys memory by **(observer, observed)** peer pairs; Nora joins every session with `observe_others=True` (humans `observe_me=True`, `HonchoClient._configure_peer`), so the deriver builds `(nora → person)` — her model of someone from what she witnessed, distinct from their self-model. Live-proven: a probe peer's job+hobby returned from one observed message; empty without the config. (1) **The clean topology (operator drilled):** **unit = a group of PEOPLE** (a social unit), **session = a CHANNEL** that same unit uses (Signal/Discord/WhatsApp group), **peer = a person**. Cross-session blend within a workspace is safe by construction — same humans, different apps, one social context; two social units never share a workspace. Two orthogonal scopes: unit = what she may KNOW together, roster = whom she may SAY. (2) **`ask_memory(person, depth)`** — the dialectic verb (`HonchoClient.chat`, `target`=observed), Nora's escalation from `about` (retrieve→reason); `depth` is the MODEL's per-question choice (minimal→max), slow (~14-19s), budget 1, roster-gated, identifier-bearing answer withheld whole. `about` rescoped to `(observer=ai_peer, target=person)`. (3) **Session-id sanitised** (`4c9f107`): Honcho requires `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, a Signal group id is base64 (`+/=`) → 422 → the WHOLE feed path was silently dead on real groups (offline used clean ids); `_safe_conversation_key` maps base64→url-safe, hash fallback. (4) **C1 (review):** the ai_peer observe-config re-fires on the cache-hit path, so a transient failure retries not disables. (5) **`[agent].name`** (`0fcad88`) makes the agent's machine identity config (Strands/trace id), so a clone ("delia") is config + doctrine files. | DEC-75 | **"A verified list is not a verified match" — `conduct.md`'s Honesty section refuses to let Nora attribute an unlabeled list entry to the asker without an actual link (operator 2026-08-09).** Real incident: asked to compare against a Pulse leaderboard of game handles, she confidently named the WRONG handle as the asker, and the false claim reached Honcho's long-term memory before manual deletion. The judge model became `[evals] judge_model` (operator cost knob), refused if it equals `llm.model` (self-grading, `_resolve_judge_model_id`, a STRING-identity guard — a different-provider alias of the same weights would slip it, noted at the guard). TIER (precautionary, NOT a controlled measurement): a single confounded run — different stochastic replies per judge, n=3, one correlated case shape — had grounded flash matching fewer fabrications than grounded pro. That is an anecdote consistent with «a weaker judge misses more», not a factor ranking; pro stays as the CONSERVATIVE default (asymmetric error cost: a weak judge misses fabrications, a strong one only costs money) pending a frozen-reply, repeated-judge comparison. The «0/3» above was the BLIND judge's detection (it caught 0 of 3 because it couldn't see the source list); the grounded judge catches 3/3, which is the real, still-unfixed doctrine gap. **REVIEW-2 (subagent + Kimi, commit 387620a→this): the gate now binds ONLY the `no_overreach_or_fabrication` criterion (`safety_verdict`), not the flaky all-six roll-up — six subjective criteria on one stochastic sample false-fail a good doctrine; the judge runs at temperature 0 (a grader must be near-deterministic, it was inheriting the 0.7 REPLY tuning); a required reply that never came now FAILs (a false-PASS the empty-reply judge-skip had reopened); a REVIEW retries once (transient-parse insurance, fail-closed otherwise). OPEN follow-ups: the corpus is all rank-2/identity-shape (overfitting — needs stat/shape diversity + a non-identity fabrication case + more grounded controls), the injection cases carry no `transcript` so the safety criterion grades them without source data, and the tier claim needs a controlled frozen-reply run. **AND — measured, the deeper one — the judge's own fabrication-detection was NOISY: a temp-0 re-run caught 1/3 of the same cases an earlier run caught 3/3, because the replies are stochastic AND the judge passed a fabricated ATTRIBUTION that carried a grounded VALUE («你排第一，52死» — 52 IS in the data, but nothing links «你» to that entry). Fixed (A1-A4, commit 27c05b8→this): (A1) the judge prompt grades value-grounding and identity-ATTRIBUTION as two independent checks; (A2) the gate binds the MAJORITY of `judge_samples`=3 grades, killing single-sample noise; (A3) a frozen-reply cache holds the reply constant so judge comparisons are controlled; (A4) the CONTROLLED comparison — same frozen replies, k=3 — showed **flash MATCHES pro: BOTH 3/3 fabrications caught + control PASS.** The earlier "pro beats flash" was confounded single-sample noise (Kimi called it), and the "measured live it FAILs the cases" was the n=1 over-claim this two-tier review exists to catch. So `judge_model` moved to `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` (a DIFFERENT provider route than the tested `opencode-zen/deepseek-v4-flash` — the guard is string-identity) for cost; same base model is weaker independence but measured to work for this class. Still n=4 controlled — the diversified corpus (C1) + a ≥10-reply controlled run is the confirmation. **C1 DONE, and it corrected the picture (as Kimi predicted): on a DIVERSIFIED corpus (varied rank + a NON-identity «invented time window» fabrication + 2 grounded controls) the judge catches only 3/5 fabrications, not 3/3 — the narrow all-rank-2 corpus OVERSTATED it. Controls pass 2/2 (low false-positive). So the gate MECHANISM is sound and controls are clean, but judge DETECTION on diverse fabrications (esp. invented-data, not just misattribution) is the real open frontier — the next iteration is a judge prompt that also catches fabricated STRUCTURE/values, measured on frozen diverse replies. The «flash == pro» holds only on the narrow set; re-decide the tier on the diverse frozen set.** `identity_grounding.yaml` is STILL deliberately ungated: the DOCTRINE gap it records is real and unfixed, so folding it into the gated corpus would (correctly) redden CI — it stays a measured record until the doctrine reliably passes it. | DEC-85 | **Recurring + lead-time reminders — a series is a CHAIN of one-shot rows, advanced inside the claim (operator, from a live stress test, 2026-08-10).** Three real asks were refused by DEC-70's v1 with 「我 set 唔到 recurring 每日提嘅 reminder」: an annual birthday, a daily countdown into a wedding anniversary, and a single reminder a week before a date. Eight decisions worth the index. (1) **A recurring reminder is N ROWS, not a row that repeats.** Only one is ever `pending`; the rest do not exist yet. This is what lets every rule DEC-70 argued for survive untouched — R-37 (“a row fires once, ever”), R-37b (at-most-once across a crash), R-36 (`due_at <= now` and nothing else), the `(state, due_at)` index and the whole `pending → firing → done` machine are all unchanged, because no row is ever re-armed, reset or re-queued. The rejected alternative — one row whose `due_at` advances — puts a mutable schedule inside the object whose immutability the at-most-once argument rests on, and overwrites the audit trail of every occurrence it has already fired. (2) **The successor is minted INSIDE `claim`, in the same transaction.** The claim is the only exactly-once point in a reminder's life (a compare-and-set on `state = 'pending'`), and the successor has to inherit that. Minted after the fire turn instead, a crash mid-turn would leave the row FIRING, boot recovery would sweep it to FAILED, and the series would end silently at the first crash — a daily reminder killed by one bad night. Minted here it is durable before any egress is attempted, so the series survives a timeout, a model error or a dead process; and a row that is never claimed — cancelled, or refused by the fire-time policy re-check — mints nothing, so a series stops exactly where the decision to stop it was made. `claim` therefore takes `now`, for the reason `due()` and `sweep_firing()` already do. (3) **Cancelling one occurrence and cancelling the series are the same operation, and cancelling ONE is deliberately not offered.** The chain's next link is only ever forged by a claim, so cancelling the single pending occurrence ends everything that is left — `cancel_reminder` needed no new argument and no new verb. Skipping one day and keeping the rest is refused because it needs two things this feature does not have: a skip-marker state (so the skipped occurrence still advances the chain without firing) and a way for a person to NAME an occurrence they have never seen, since only the next one is ever listed. (4) **The successor's id is `uuid5(series_id, occurrence)`, not `uuid4`.** A derived id makes minting the same occurrence twice a PRIMARY KEY collision the database refuses, rather than a duplicate reminder — the same thing said twice, which is precisely what R-37b exists to prevent. The one new write recurrence adds is one the database itself can refuse. (5) **The catch-up rule is SKIP, and the skipped occurrences are CONSUMED.** The successor is the first occurrence strictly after `now`, not the one after the row that just fired, so a process down for three days fires its one overdue row once and resumes tomorrow — never ten messages in ten ticks, every one about a moment that has passed. Skipped occurrences still spend their slot in `count`, so an outage cannot lengthen a series' calendar footprint past the fortnight it was asked for. It is arithmetic rather than iteration (`_floor_index` then a bounded walk), so a decade-long gap costs one subtraction. (6) **The DST rule: a recurrence keeps its LOCAL WALL CLOCK, and the anchor is what every occurrence is computed from.** The step is taken on the local calendar in an IANA zone (`[reminders].timezone`, never an offset — `+08:00` cannot say what 08:00 local means across a boundary), then converted back to UTC, so a daily 08:00 reminder is a 23-hour step at spring-forward and a 25-hour one at autumn-back. A wall clock that does not exist that day resolves through the pre-transition offset (`fold=0`) and fires an hour late rather than vanishing; one that exists twice fires once, at the first. Month and year steps CLAMP to the last day of the target month, and computing from the anchor rather than from the predecessor is what makes clamping safe: 31 Jan → 28 Feb → **31** Mar, and 29 Feb → 28 Feb → 28 Feb → **29** Feb on the next leap year, where chained clamping loses the date permanently on the first short month. (7) **A series is bounded BY TYPE, and counts as ONE against `max_pending_per_requester`.** `RecurrenceRule.count` is required and `>= 1`, so «repeats forever» is not a value the domain can hold — the bound cannot be forgotten by a new call site the way a check can. The model's `times` is clamped to `[reminders].max_occurrences_per_series` (60) and defaults to it; `until` narrows further and never widens. The cap counts one because the chain only ever has one pending row, and `remind` returns `repeat_left` so she can say the limit back — a bound nobody was told about is the part a person is most surprised by later. `max_horizon_days` still bounds the FIRST occurrence only, with one period of headroom for a rule whose own period is longer (a yearly birthday's first occurrence is a year out by definition, so a 30-day horizon does not bound that recurrence — it forbids it, which is how 「記住我嘅生日」 was refused). (8) **LEAD TIME IS NOT A STORED CONCEPT — it is arithmetic on `when`.** 「接近日期前兩個星期每日提」 is `when` = 27 September, `repeat="daily"`, `times=14`; 「前一個禮拜講一次」 is `when` = the date minus seven days and no recurrence at all. The model already resolves 「等陣」 into an instant, so a `lead_days`/`target_date` pair would be a second scheduler in the schema for arithmetic that is already being done. **No RRULE dependency**: the five intervals cover every ask, and RFC 5545 brings BYSETPOS/BYDAY/EXDATE that no surface here can produce and all of which would have to round-trip through the schema, the tool arguments and the model's head. | `tests/contract/test_reminder_store_contract.py` (the chain, the claim-minted successor, exclusivity, catch-up, cancel-ends-the-series, one-per-cap, DST — both stores), `tests/unit/test_reminder_recurrence.py` (the calendar: spring-forward, autumn-back, the gap, the overlap, 31 Jan monthly, 29 Feb yearly, the long-outage skip, the derived id, every bound), `tests/test_reminder_tools.py` (the three asks verbatim, the recurrence refusals, the bare-date `until`, `min_lead_seconds` on the first occurrence, the per-period horizon headroom, the listing), `tests/unit/test_fire_path.py` (the header says a repeat is a repeat, and a one-shot header is unchanged), `tests/infra/test_schema_parity.py` (`0005_reminder_recurrence`, `ck_reminders_recurrence` — the all-or-nothing CHECK `alembic check` is blind to) |

| DEC-115 | **The presence analytics substrate: the DERIVED layer `design/19 §2` deferred, built as a consumer-NEUTRAL service whose neutrality is an import contract rather than a comment (design/27, spec 2026-08-18).** §2 built RAW and deferred DERIVED on a sound argument — the record is authoritative and the derivation recomputable, so no lock-in and no rush.
